goal: Arduino Uno fire alarm that senses heat and the light of flames: a 10k NTC thermistor and a 10k resistor as a voltage divider into A0 for temperature, a photoresistor (LDR) and a 10k resistor as a voltage divider into A1 for light, a passive piezo buzzer on D8 and a red 5 mm LED on D13 through a 220 ohm resistor. When the temperature goes above 50 C, or it gets hotter and much brighter at the same time, the LED flashes and the buzzer sounds an alarm. It prints the temperature and light level to the Serial Monitor.

plan.title: Dual Heat and Flame Light Fire Alarm with Arduino Uno
plan.summary: This project builds an intelligent early-warning fire alarm that monitors both ambient temperature and sudden increases in light from flames. An NTC thermistor and a photoresistor (LDR) form voltage dividers feeding analog signals to an Arduino Uno, while a red LED and piezo buzzer alert you when fire conditions are detected. Real-time temperature and ambient light readings are continuously sent to the Serial Monitor.
plan.final_result: When powered via USB, the Arduino constantly logs the ambient temperature (°C) and light level to the Serial Monitor. Under normal conditions the LED and buzzer remain quiet. When the temperature exceeds 50 °C, or if sudden heat and bright flame light occur simultaneously, the red LED flashes urgently and the piezo buzzer emits an audible siren alarm.

tests.title: Test the red warning LED
tests.what_it_tests: Checks the external red LED, its current-limiting resistor, and its connections to pin 13 and ground.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. The red LED on the breadboard should light for half a second, then go dark for half a second, repeatedly. The Uno's built-in LED may blink too. Unplug USB before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: Check step 3: the LED's long leg belongs in e10 and its short leg in e11. Check step 4: the 220 ohm resistor connects d11 to d15. Check step 5: a10 connects to digital pin 13. Check steps 1 and 6: Arduino GND connects to the top ground rail next to row 1, and a15 connects to that same rail next to row 15.

tests.title: Test the piezo buzzer
tests.what_it_tests: Checks that the piezo buzzer can produce a tone through pin 8 and its ground connection.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. The buzzer should make a short, high-pitched beep for a quarter of a second, followed by three-quarters of a second of silence, repeatedly. Unplug USB before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: Check step 7: the buzzer's positive leg is in e20 and its negative leg in e23. Check step 8: a20 connects to Arduino digital pin 8. Check step 9: a23 connects to the top ground rail next to row 23. Check step 1: that ground rail connects to Arduino GND.

tests.title: Test the thermistor reading
tests.what_it_tests: Checks that the thermistor voltage divider supplies a temperature-responsive signal to analog pin A0.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. Open the Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. It should print lines such as "Thermistor A0: 512" twice per second; the exact value depends on temperature. Gently warm the thermistor between your fingers: the number should gradually increase, then decrease as it cools after release. Do not use a flame. Unplug USB before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: Check step 10: the thermistor spans e30 and e31. Check step 11: the 10k ohm resistor spans d31 and d35. Check step 12: a30 connects to the positive rail next to row 30. Check step 13: a31 connects to A0. Check step 14: a35 connects to the ground rail next to row 35. Check steps 1–2: the top rails connect to Arduino GND and 5V next to row 1. If a rail is split between row 1 and the sensor connections, its sections need to be connected before this test can work.

safety: Always disconnect the Arduino USB cable before plugging in or rearranging any components and wires on the breadboard.
Do not use an open flame directly on the breadboard or against the sensors; test by bringing a warm hand, warm air from a hairdryer, or flashlight near the sensors.
Ensure the 220 ohm resistor is always in series with the LED to prevent overloading the Arduino digital output pin.

part_guide.breadboard_1: A breadboard is a reusable board for building circuits without soldering: you push part legs and wires into its holes, and metal strips hidden inside connect them. In each numbered row, the five holes on one side of the middle groove are joined, and the long lines of holes along the edges (the rails) share power or ground with the whole board.
part_guide.arduino_uno: An Arduino Uno is a small programmable board: you load a program onto it from your computer over USB, and it turns its pins on and off or reads sensors. Here it watches the heat and light sensors and sounds the alarm when both look like a fire. Its pins are the black sockets along the edges, each with a printed label.
part_guide.led_red: An LED is a small light. This red one flashes when the alarm goes off. It only works one way round: the longer leg goes to + and the shorter leg, beside the flat edge of its rim, goes to −.
part_guide.res_led: A resistor is a tiny striped part that limits how much electricity flows. This one protects the LED from too much current, which would burn it out. It works either way round; a 220 Ω one has red, red, brown bands.
part_guide.buzzer_1: A piezo buzzer is a small round disc that beeps when the Uno sends it a signal. Here it is the alarm sound. Its + leg is the slightly longer one, also marked + on top.
part_guide.thermistor_1: A thermistor is a temperature sensor: a small dark bead on two thin legs whose resistance drops as it heats up. It tells the Uno how hot it is. It works either way round.
part_guide.res_therm: A resistor is a tiny striped part that limits how much electricity flows. This 10 kΩ one (brown, black, orange bands) pairs with the thermistor so the Uno sees a voltage that changes with temperature.
part_guide.ldr_1: A light sensor (photoresistor): a small disc with a squiggly line on its face, whose resistance falls in bright light. Here it notices the glow of a flame. It works either way round.
part_guide.res_ldr: A resistor is a tiny striped part that limits how much electricity flows. This 10 kΩ one (brown, black, orange bands) pairs with the light sensor so the Uno sees a voltage that changes with the light.
part_guide.wire_main_gnd: The black wire joins the Uno's GND pin (ground: the 0 V side every part returns its current to) to the ground rail along the top edge, which all the parts share.
part_guide.wire_main_5v: The red wire brings 5 V power from the Uno's 5V pin to the + rail along the top edge, so both sensors can take power from it.
part_guide.wire_led_sig: The orange wire carries the on/off signal from the Uno's pin 13 to the LED's longer leg.
part_guide.wire_led_gnd: The black wire runs from the LED's resistor up to the ground rail, completing the LED's loop.
part_guide.wire_buzzer_sig: The blue wire carries the alarm sound signal from the Uno's pin 8 to the buzzer's + leg.
part_guide.wire_buzzer_gnd: The black wire joins the buzzer's other leg to the ground rail, completing its circuit.
part_guide.wire_therm_vcc: The red wire brings 5 V from the + rail to one leg of the thermistor.
part_guide.wire_therm_sig: The green wire carries the temperature reading, from between the thermistor and its resistor, to the Uno's pin A0, which measures voltage.
part_guide.wire_therm_gnd: The black wire connects the thermistor's 10 kΩ resistor to the ground rail, completing the temperature sensor's circuit.
part_guide.wire_ldr_vcc: The red wire brings 5 V from the + rail to one leg of the light sensor.
part_guide.wire_ldr_sig: The yellow wire carries the light reading, from between the light sensor and its resistor, to the Uno's pin A1.
part_guide.wire_ldr_gnd: The black wire connects the light sensor's 10 kΩ resistor to the ground rail, completing its circuit.

steps.instruction: Insert a 10k ohm resistor (color bands brown-black-orange) with lead 1 in row 31, column d, and lead 2 in row 35, column d.
steps.check: A 10k resistor spans from row 31, column d to row 35, column d.
steps.why: This resistor helps turn temperature changes into a signal the Arduino can read.

steps.title: Power the Thermistor
steps.instruction: Plug one end of a red jumper wire into the positive (+) power rail along the top edge next to row 30, and plug the other end into row 30, column a.

placements.where: the inner positive rail along the top edge, next to row 30

steps.check: A red wire connects the inner top 5V power rail next to row 30 to row 30, column a.
steps.why: This supplies power to the temperature sensor.

steps.title: Wire Thermistor Junction to Analog Pin A0
steps.instruction: Plug one end of a green jumper wire into row 31, column a, and plug the other end into Arduino analog header pin labelled A0.

placements.where: Arduino analog header pin labelled A0

steps.check: A green wire runs between row 31, column a and Arduino analog pin A0.
steps.why: This lets the Arduino read the temperature signal.

steps.title: Ground the Thermistor Divider
steps.instruction: Plug one end of a black jumper wire into row 35, column a, and plug the other end straight up into the ground rail along the top edge next to row 35.

placements.where: the outer ground rail along the top edge, next to row 35

steps.check: A black wire links row 35, column a directly up to the top ground rail at row 35.
steps.why: This completes the temperature sensor’s path back to the power supply.

steps.title: Insert Photoresistor (LDR)
steps.instruction: Insert the photoresistor into column e: place one lead in row 40, column e, and place the other lead in row 41, column e.
steps.check: The photoresistor faces upward with leads inserted into e40 and e41.
steps.why: This part senses changes in brightness that may come from flames.

steps.title: Insert Photoresistor 10k Resistor
steps.instruction: Insert the second 10k ohm resistor (color bands brown-black-orange) with lead 1 in row 41, column d, and lead 2 in row 45, column d.
steps.check: A 10k resistor bridges row 41, column d to row 45, column d.
steps.why: This resistor helps turn brightness changes into a signal the Arduino can read.

steps.title: Power the Photoresistor
steps.instruction: Plug one end of a red jumper wire into the positive (+) power rail along the top edge next to row 40, and plug the other end into row 40, column a.

placements.where: the inner positive rail along the top edge, next to row 40

steps.check: A red wire connects the inner top 5V rail next to row 40 to row 40, column a.
steps.why: This supplies power to the light sensor.

steps.title: Wire Photoresistor Junction to Analog Pin A1
steps.instruction: Plug one end of a yellow jumper wire into row 41, column a, and plug the other end into Arduino analog header pin labelled A1.

placements.where: Arduino analog header pin labelled A1

steps.check: A yellow wire connects row 41, column a to Arduino analog pin A1.
steps.why: This lets the Arduino read the brightness signal.

steps.title: Ground the Photoresistor Divider
steps.instruction: Plug one end of a black jumper wire into row 45, column a, and plug the other end straight up into the ground rail along the top edge next to row 45.

placements.where: the outer ground rail along the top edge, next to row 45

steps.check: A black wire links row 45, column a directly up to the top ground rail at row 45.
steps.why: This completes the light sensor’s path back to the power supply.

plan.final_result: When powered via USB, the Arduino constantly logs the ambient temperature (°C) and light level to the Serial Monitor. Under normal conditions the LED and buzzer remain quiet. When the temperature exceeds 50 °C, or if sudden heat and bright flame light occur simultaneously, the red LED flashes urgently and the piezo buzzer emits an audible siren alarm.
safety: Always disconnect the Arduino USB cable before plugging in or rearranging any components and wires on the breadboard.
Do not use an open flame directly on the breadboard or against the sensors; test by bringing a warm hand, warm air from a hairdryer, or flashlight near the sensors.
Ensure the 220 ohm resistor is always in series with the LED to prevent overloading the Arduino digital output pin.

tests.title: Test the red warning LED
tests.what_it_tests: Checks the external red LED, its current-limiting resistor, and its connections to pin 13 and ground.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. The red LED on the breadboard should light for half a second, then go dark for half a second, repeatedly. The Uno's built-in LED may blink too. Unplug USB before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: Check step 3: the LED's long leg belongs in e10 and its short leg in e11. Check step 4: the 220 ohm resistor connects d11 to d15. Check step 5: a10 connects to digital pin 13. Check steps 1 and 6: Arduino GND connects to the top ground rail next to row 1, and a15 connects to that same rail next to row 15.

tests.title: Test the piezo buzzer
tests.what_it_tests: Checks that the piezo buzzer can produce a tone through pin 8 and its ground connection.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. The buzzer should make a short, high-pitched beep for a quarter of a second, followed by three-quarters of a second of silence, repeatedly. Unplug USB before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: Check step 7: the buzzer's positive leg is in e20 and its negative leg in e23. Check step 8: a20 connects to Arduino digital pin 8. Check step 9: a23 connects to the top ground rail next to row 23. Check step 1: that ground rail connects to Arduino GND.

tests.title: Test the thermistor reading
tests.what_it_tests: Checks that the thermistor voltage divider supplies a temperature-responsive signal to analog pin A0.
tests.expect: Plug in the USB cable and upload this sketch. Open the Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. It should print lines such as "Thermistor A0: 512" twice per second; the exact value depends on temperature. Gently warm the thermistor between your fingers: the number should gradually increase, then decrease as it cools after release. Do not use a flame. Unplug USB before continuing the build.
tests.if_not: Check step 10: the thermistor spans e30 and e31. Check step 11: the 10k ohm resistor spans d31 and d35. Check step 12: a30 connects to the positive rail next to row 30. Check step 13: a31 connects to A0. Check step 14: a35 connects to the ground rail next to row 35. Check steps 1–2: the top rails connect to Arduino GND and 5V next to row 1. If a rail is split between row 1 and the sensor connections, its sections need to be connected before this test can work.
